articles.title: Women ‘first to suffer’ under siege, first to step up as frontline responders in Sudan
articles.summary: When Tahani Al-Numeiri heard the first explosions in Khartoum, her hometown, war seemed so remote that she assumed they were celebrations from a nearby wedding. It was the morning of 15 April 2023, and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces had just turned their guns on the army.
articles.content:
Large-scale conflict had only ever been either something that happened to others, or the stuff of fiction.

“I never imagined my life would turn out just like in the movie,” she says.

Yet for her and millions of Sudanese people, it came knocking on their front door as the war between rival militaries erupted three and a half years ago, triggering one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises.

In the face of mass displacement, hunger, and psychosocial trauma, some women – spotlighted by gender equality agency, UN Women – rolled up their sleeves and emerged as key frontline responders.

Inside besieged Khartoum

Ms. Al-Numeiri and her family were one of the many who found themselves trapped in areas taken under siege.

In their case, they got stuck in Khartoum, which was disputed between the two main combatants – the RSF and the military government’s Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF).

Ms. Al-Numeiri, a journalist and activist, remembers how communication networks collapsed, banking services became inaccessible and essential supplies disappeared.

They were left with nothing to eat except boiled wheat, and they had to burn their furniture to keep themselves warm when fuel ran out.

Malnutrition, contaminated water and lack of medical care caused her to fall critically ill.

“My body was swollen, my skin was peeling, scabs were coming off. I had a severe fever, and there was blood in my eyes. I could not even see anyone next to me. My family had given up. They said I was going to die,” she said.

© UNICEF/Mohammed Jamal

Standing back up

“Sunset came, then night, and I found myself still alive in my room”, says Ms. Al-Numeiri.

After Khartoum was retaken by government troops in March 2025, and as she recovered, she turned to help others in her community who had also lived and suffered under the siege.

As she was collecting food for her family from a communal kitchen – a meagre two spoons of lentils – the woman running the kitchen found out she was a journalist and encouraged her to post online about the conditions families in the city were living in.

She soon became a volunteer at the kitchen herself and documented the impact of the war on women and children in videos that went viral online – in effect raising awareness and support for those in need in Sudan.

“I feel like I am a warrior on the frontlines,” she says.

Women ‘first to suffer’ in El Fasher

Hundreds of miles away in the southwest of Khartoum, the city of El Fasher was also besieged by the RSF in October 2025.

Amna Mohamed*, the President of a women-led and UN-supported organization that provides meals and financial support to women in need in North Darfur, stayed in the city to continue helping her community.

Many were unable to flee – notably those who were caring for elderly relatives, persons with disabilities or other dependents who were unable to travel, and those who did not have the money to hire a donkey or other mode of transportation to leave.

All endure severe food shortages, soaring prices, lack of healthcare and bombardments, but Mohamed stressed that “women were the first to suffer”.

“They may beat or rape you, and sometimes they loot your belongings. Sometimes they demand that you leave your home; they may kill your husband or brothers right before your eyes, or they may take your daughters right in front of you and lead them away to unknown locations,” she said.

“Our relationship with women is direct and close, and as women-led organizations, we are best positioned to serve them; we understand their needs. However, when it comes to funding, projects sometimes go to organizations led by men,” she explained.

Psychological scars

Back in Khartoum, thousands of women are returning after being displaced for years across Sudan and in neighbouring countries.

Yet for many, while the end of one difficult chapter, coming home is only the start of another.

Many are dealing with trauma from the early stages of the war and from their displacement, and they have come back to looted houses, stripped of everything they owned – even doors and windows.

“After they returned home, women came back with nothing in their hands, they lost everything”, explains Israa Hamid Khalil, a psychological support officer at the UN Women-supported East Nile Women’s Empowerment Centre in the capital city.

The centre offers counselling and psychological care, as well as training and livelihood support to enable them to earn an income and support their families.

“Women returned to the place where they had experienced those painful memories and traumas. They can’t just stay at home and keep reliving those things.

“We now address this challenge: How can we help them overcome this stage and begin their journey of psychological recovery?” said Ms. Khalil.

*name changed to protect her identity

The story is substantive and inspiring, emphasizing hope and empowerment amid crisis.
articles.personality_title: Sudanese women lead recovery and support amid war hardships
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Since April 2023, Sudan has been caught in a violent conflict between two military groups, causing severe suffering and a humanitarian crisis. Cities like Khartoum and El Fasher have been under siege, with many families trapped without food, water, or medical care.

**What happened** – Women in Sudan, such as journalist Tahani Al-Numeiri and activist Amna Mohamed, have taken on important roles during the conflict. Despite facing hunger, illness, and danger, they became frontline helpers by volunteering in kitchens, sharing news to raise awareness, and providing meals and financial aid to others in need.

**Impact** – These women-led efforts have brought crucial support to communities where many people, especially women, suffered violence, loss, and trauma. For example, Tahani’s videos helped spread the reality of the war’s effect on families, increasing aid and attention. Women’s organizations also understand the specific needs of women survivors and are working to offer both practical help and psychological support.

**What's next step** – As fighting slows and displaced people return home, programs like the East Nile Women’s Empowerment Centre are helping women recover mentally and rebuild their lives. They offer counseling and training to help women earn money and support their families, aiming to heal the deep emotional wounds caused by the war.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Despite facing extreme hardship, Sudanese women have become vital leaders in helping their communities survive and recover from war.
articles.personality_title_fr: Des femmes soudanaises en première ligne pour la reconstruction après la guerre
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Depuis avril 2023, le Soudan est plongé dans un conflit violent entre deux groupes militaires, provoquant de grandes souffrances et une crise humanitaire. Des villes comme Khartoum et El Fasher ont été assiégées, laissant de nombreuses familles sans nourriture, eau ni soins médicaux.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des femmes soudanaises, comme la journaliste Tahani Al-Numeiri et l’activiste Amna Mohamed, ont joué un rôle important pendant le conflit. Malgré la faim, la maladie et le danger, elles sont devenues des aides essentielles en servant dans des cuisines communautaires, en partageant des informations pour sensibiliser, et en fournissant repas et soutien financier.

**Impact** – Ces actions menées par des femmes ont apporté un soutien crucial aux communautés où beaucoup, surtout des femmes, ont subi violences, pertes et traumatismes. Par exemple, les vidéos de Tahani ont permis de montrer au monde la réalité de la guerre, ce qui a aidé à attirer plus d’aide. Les organisations féminines comprennent mieux les besoins spécifiques des survivantes et offrent aussi un soutien psychologique.

**Prochaine étape** – Alors que les combats diminuent et que les personnes déplacées rentrent chez elles, des programmes comme le Centre d’autonomisation des femmes de East Nile aident les femmes à se reconstruire mentalement et à retrouver une vie stable. Ils proposent des conseils et des formations pour qu’elles puissent gagner leur vie et soutenir leur famille.

**En une phrase** – Malgré des difficultés extrêmes, les femmes soudanaises sont devenues des leaders essentiels pour aider leurs communautés à survivre et se relever après la guerre.
articles.personality_title_es: Mujeres sudanesas lideran la recuperación y apoyo en medio del conflicto
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Desde abril de 2023, Sudán ha estado en un conflicto violento entre dos grupos militares, causando gran sufrimiento y una crisis humanitaria. Ciudades como Jartum y El Fasher han estado sitiadas, dejando a muchas familias sin comida, agua ni atención médica.

**Qué pasó** – Mujeres sudanesas, como la periodista Tahani Al-Numeiri y la activista Amna Mohamed, han asumido roles importantes durante el conflicto. A pesar del hambre, la enfermedad y el peligro, se convirtieron en ayudantes clave, trabajando en cocinas comunitarias, compartiendo información para crear conciencia y brindando comidas y apoyo financiero.

**Impacto** – Estos esfuerzos liderados por mujeres han dado un apoyo vital a comunidades donde muchas personas, especialmente mujeres, sufrieron violencia, pérdidas y traumas. Por ejemplo, los videos de Tahani ayudaron a mostrar la realidad de la guerra, lo que aumentó la ayuda y la atención. Las organizaciones de mujeres también entienden mejor las necesidades específicas de las sobrevivientes y ofrecen apoyo psicológico.

**Próximo paso** – A medida que los combates disminuyen y las personas desplazadas regresan a sus hogares, programas como el Centro de Empoderamiento de Mujeres East Nile ayudan a las mujeres a recuperarse mentalmente y reconstruir sus vidas. Ofrecen consejería y capacitación para que puedan ganar dinero y mantener a sus familias.

**Resumen en una frase** – A pesar de grandes dificultades, las mujeres sudanesas se han convertido en líderes esenciales para ayudar a sus comunidades a sobrevivir y recuperarse después de la guerra.

articles.title: Students like new tenancy freedoms - but landlords warn of higher rents
articles.summary: The Renters' Rights Act gives greater flexibility to leave a tenancy but the changes have posed challenges for student landlords.
articles.content:
When the Renters' Rights Act came into force in May it was described as the biggest change for tenants in England in a generation, giving more stability and security to the millions of people who rent from private landlords.

The legislation has also prompted a shake-up of the student rental market, which has posed challenges for landlords as it allows people to leave a tenancy rather than being tied in for the full academic year.

Eddie Lever had finished his first year at the University of Exeter when he decided the course wasn't for him.

The 20-year-old wanted to switch to studying international relations at the University of York but had already organised his house for the upcoming year.

The tenancy was signed and had started.

But because of changes in the Renters' Rights Act, Eddie only had to give two months' notice before he could leave and stop paying rent.

The legislation ended fixed-term tenancies - where renters are tied in to contracts for a specific number of months. For students, previously contracts were generally for the full academic year.

Instead, properties are now rented on a rolling basis, which means tenants pay rent weekly or monthly with no fixed end date.

University-owned halls of residence and Purpose-Built Student Accommodation are exempt, external and can still offer fixed-term contracts so this change primarily affects students renting from a private landlord.

"If the Renters' Rights Act wasn't a thing, I don't think I would have been able to move universities because I would have been locked into the full [year] contract," Eddie explains.

"It would have made it unaffordable."
articles.reasoning: The Renters' Rights Act introduces significant tenant protections by ending fixed-term tenancies, allowing renters (including students) greater flexibility and security. This legislative change positively impacts millions of renters in England by improving housing stability and affordability, representing a meaningful advancement in tenant rights with broad societal benefits.
articles.personality_title: New renter laws give students more freedom to change homes
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – In May, England introduced the Renters' Rights Act, a new law changing how rental agreements work. Before this law, many renters, including students, had to stay in their homes for a fixed time, usually an entire year.

**What happened** – The law ended fixed-term tenancies for most private rentals, allowing tenants to pay rent weekly or monthly without a set end date. This means renters can leave their homes more easily by giving just two months' notice. For example, Eddie Lever, a student who wanted to switch universities, could leave his rented house without paying rent for the full year because of this change.

**Impact** – This change gives renters, especially students, more control over where they live and when they move. It helps them avoid paying for housing they no longer need, making renting fairer and more affordable. However, it mainly affects private rentals, not university dorms or special student housing, which still use fixed contracts.

**What's next step** – Landlords will need to adjust to these flexible agreements, which some say might lead to higher rents to cover risks. Students and other renters will likely benefit from more choices and protections, while landlords consider new ways to manage their properties.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The Renters' Rights Act gives students and renters more freedom to leave homes when they need, improving flexibility and fairness in England’s rental market.
articles.personality_title_fr: La nouvelle loi sur les locataires offre plus de liberté aux étudiants
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – En mai, l'Angleterre a adopté la loi sur les droits des locataires, qui change la façon dont fonctionnent les contrats de location. Avant cette loi, de nombreux locataires, notamment les étudiants, devaient rester dans leur logement pour une durée fixe, souvent une année entière.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – La loi a supprimé les baux à durée déterminée pour la plupart des locations privées, permettant aux locataires de payer le loyer chaque semaine ou chaque mois sans date de fin précise. Cela signifie qu'ils peuvent quitter leur logement plus facilement en donnant seulement deux mois de préavis. Par exemple, Eddie Lever, un étudiant souhaitant changer d’université, a pu quitter sa maison louée sans payer pour toute l’année grâce à ce changement.

**Impact** – Ce changement donne aux locataires, surtout aux étudiants, plus de contrôle sur leur logement et leur déménagement. Cela les aide à éviter de payer pour un logement dont ils n'ont plus besoin, rendant la location plus juste et abordable. Cependant, cela concerne surtout les locations privées, car les résidences universitaires et logements étudiants spéciaux gardent des contrats fixes.

**Prochaine étape** – Les propriétaires devront s’adapter à ces contrats plus flexibles, ce qui pourrait entraîner une hausse des loyers pour couvrir les risques. Les étudiants et autres locataires bénéficieront probablement de plus de choix et de protections, tandis que les propriétaires chercheront de nouvelles façons de gérer leurs biens.

**Une phrase clé** – La loi sur les droits des locataires offre aux étudiants et locataires plus de liberté pour quitter leur logement quand ils le souhaitent, améliorant la flexibilité et l’équité du marché locatif en Angleterre.
articles.personality_title_es: La nueva ley de alquileres da más libertad a los estudiantes
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – En mayo, Inglaterra introdujo la Ley de Derechos de los Inquilinos, que cambia cómo funcionan los contratos de alquiler. Antes, muchos inquilinos, incluidos estudiantes, tenían que quedarse en su vivienda por un tiempo fijo, generalmente un año entero.

**Qué pasó** – La ley eliminó los contratos de duración fija para la mayoría de los alquileres privados, permitiendo que los inquilinos paguen semanal o mensualmente sin una fecha fija de finalización. Esto significa que pueden dejar su vivienda más fácilmente con solo avisar con dos meses de anticipación. Por ejemplo, Eddie Lever, un estudiante que quería cambiar de universidad, pudo dejar su casa alquilada sin pagar por todo el año gracias a este cambio.

**Impacto** – Este cambio da a los inquilinos, especialmente a los estudiantes, más control sobre dónde viven y cuándo se mudan. Les ayuda a evitar pagar por una vivienda que ya no necesitan, haciendo el alquiler más justo y accesible. Sin embargo, afecta principalmente a los alquileres privados, ya que las residencias universitarias y alojamientos especiales para estudiantes siguen con contratos fijos.

**Próximo paso** – Los propietarios tendrán que adaptarse a estos contratos flexibles, lo que algunos creen que podría aumentar los alquileres para cubrir riesgos. Los estudiantes y otros inquilinos probablemente tendrán más opciones y protecciones, mientras los propietarios buscan nuevas formas de manejar sus propiedades.

**Una frase clave** – La Ley de Derechos de los Inquilinos da a estudiantes y arrendatarios más libertad para dejar sus viviendas cuando lo necesiten, mejorando la flexibilidad y justicia en el mercado de alquiler en Inglaterra.
